nameStory: This little beetle earned its name "Asian Oak Weevil" because it originally came from Asia and has a particular fondness for munching on oak leaves. The "weevil" part comes from the Old English word "wifel," meaning beetle, and you'll know why when you see its distinctive long snout that looks like a tiny elephant trunk!
description: The Asian Oak Weevil is a small, brownish beetle about the size of a rice grain that belongs to the large family of true weevils. Like all weevils, it has a characteristic long, curved snout (called a rostrum) that extends from its head like a tiny proboscis. Adults are typically chestnut brown in color and have a somewhat oval, compact body shape. This non-native species was first discovered in North America in 1933 and has since established itself throughout much of the region.

idTips.label: Long curved snout
idTips.description: The most obvious feature is the elongated, downward-curving snout that extends from the head like a miniature elephant trunk - this rostrum is hard and feels smooth to the touch when gently examined

idTips.label: Chestnut brown color
idTips.description: Body is a warm, reddish-brown color similar to a roasted chestnut, with a slightly glossy sheen that catches light when viewed closely

idTips.label: Small oval body
idTips.description: Compact, egg-shaped body about the size of a grain of rice, feeling firm and hard when touched, with short legs tucked close underneath

idTips.label: Feeding damage pattern
idTips.description: Creates distinctive notched feeding damage along leaf edges of oak and red maple trees, leaving characteristic scalloped bite marks

idTips.label: Slow movement
idTips.description: Moves deliberately and slowly across leaves, often playing dead and dropping to the ground when disturbed, making a tiny ticking sound when it hits

habitat: Asian Oak Weevils are found wherever oak trees and red maples grow throughout New England, from suburban yards to mixed deciduous forests. Adults feed on the leaves of these trees, so look for them on the foliage during their active season. The larvae live underground, feeding on root hairs in the soil around host trees.

seasonality.spring: Adults begin emerging from overwintering sites and start feeding on newly opened oak and red maple leaves. This is when feeding damage becomes most noticeable.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when adults are most abundant and easiest to spot on host tree foliage. Look for fresh notching damage on leaf edges.
seasonality.fall: Adults continue feeding but become less active as temperatures drop. They begin seeking overwintering sites in leaf litter and bark crevices.
seasonality.winter: Adults overwinter in protected locations like leaf litter, bark cracks, and debris around the base of trees. Not typically observed during this dormant period.

funFact: Despite being called the Asian Oak Weevil, this beetle actually prefers red maple leaves over oak leaves when given a choice - scientists discovered this surprising preference through feeding studies, making its common name somewhat misleading!
confusionNotes: Asian Oak Weevils can be confused with other small brown weevils, but the combination of their chestnut-brown color and preference for feeding on oak and red maple leaves helps distinguish them. Remember: "Chestnut brown on oak crowns" - if you find a reddish-brown weevil with the classic long snout feeding on oak or maple foliage, you've likely found your Asian Oak Weevil.
contextualKnowledge: As an introduced species from Asia, the Asian Oak Weevil represents one of many non-native insects that have established themselves in New England's forests. While they can cause noticeable leaf damage, they rarely kill healthy trees outright, instead contributing to overall stress that can make trees more vulnerable to other problems.
compareHints: Since this is the only Cyrtepistomus species in our region, compare it to other common weevils like the acorn weevil, which is larger and has an even longer snout, or bark weevils, which are usually found on tree trunks rather than leaves. The Asian Oak Weevil's preference for leaf feeding and its chestnut-brown coloration help set it apart from most other weevil species in New England.
